concept.line: Every noun takes de or het: de telefoon, de bank, het boek. Learn which one with the word.
Put the verb before the subject in questions, with a question word first if needed: ‘Is dat koffie?’ or ‘Waar staat de auto?’
The verb comes second, even when the sentence starts with something other than the subject: Hier zit mijn sleutel. In mijn zak zit een sleutel.

concept.line: After want ('because'), keep the usual subject-then-verb order.
Use geen before a noun to mean 'no' or 'not a', as in geen koffie.
After dat (that), the verb goes to the end: Ik denk dat we hier kunnen eten.
A useful neutral order is time, then how, then place: we gaan vandaag met de auto naar kantoor.

concept.line: Many common verbs have a ge- form of their own, learned with the word: gegeten, gedronken, gelezen, gezien, gekocht.
Going, coming and staying take ben, not heb: Ik ben gegaan. Ik ben gekomen. Ik ben gebleven.
Some verbs come with their own preposition, and it isn't always the English one: wachten op (wait for), denken aan (think of), luisteren naar (listen to).
Before a singular noun with een, an adjective usually takes -e with a de-word but stays unchanged with a het-word.

concept.line: Dutch often makes plurals with -en or -s, sometimes with an apostrophe: boek becomes boeken and foto becomes foto's.
With a number or an amount and no noun after it, Dutch adds er, where English says of them or nothing: Ik heb er twee (I have two), Hoeveel wil je er?
Where English puts to before a verb (safe to walk, time to go), Dutch says om … te, with te and the verb at the very end: Is het veilig om hier te lopen?

concept.line: Je, we and ze are the everyday forms; jij, wij and zij are for contrast, and always when the word stands without its verb: Jullie gaan, wij niet.
When describing feelings, voelen needs a word referring back to the person: ik voel me and ze voelt zich.
A question inside a sentence keeps its question word but sends the verb to the end: Weet u waar mijn auto staat?
Little words like even, maar, toch, wel and nou add tone, not meaning: Kun je me even helpen? asks more softly than Kun je me helpen?
Use gaan or zullen with an infinitive to talk about what is going to happen.

concept.line: Zou or zouden with a verb at the end says what would happen, or asks politely: Zou je me kunnen helpen? Ik zou het niet doen.
For the past of zijn, use was with ik, je or hij and waren with we, jullie or ze meaning they.
Use er is for 'there is' and er zijn for 'there are'.
Use zijn + aan het + an infinitive to say what someone is doing right now.
Where English says to before a verb, Dutch puts te right before it, at the end: moeilijk te begrijpen, Ik hoef niets te doen.
When a sentence opens with a whole clause (als, omdat, terwijl, toen), that clause takes first place, so the main verb comes right after the comma: Als ik thuis ben, bel ik je.

concept.line: Add information with die after a de-word or a person and dat after a het-word, putting the verb or verb group at the end.
Zitten, liggen, staan or lopen with te and a verb says what someone is busy doing, and how they are while they do it: Ik zit te lezen, Hij ligt te slapen.
Had or was with a past form at the end says what had already happened before another moment in the past: Ik had al gegeten. Ze was al naar huis gegaan.
In the perfect, kunnen, moeten, willen, laten or zien stays as it is beside the other verb, both at the end: We hebben de deur open kunnen krijgen.
